solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Mark gets Oscar — he had two!

parts.note: a brand is a mark, as burned on cattle or a trade mark
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A man called Mark wins an Oscar, and we are told he has two of the statuettes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' looks like the film award but is just the letter O; the award returns in the definition, since the actor won two Academy Awards.
explanation.definitionFit: The film actor won two Academy Awards, for On the Waterfront and The Godfather, so he is the man who had two.

clue.text: Upsets monks? Not right!

indicators.note: 'Not right' asks for the letter standing for right to be left out of the monks

parts.note: monks are brothers of a religious order

explanation.surface: Someone is annoyed by monks behaving badly and exclaims that it is not right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' removes R from BROTHERS.
explanation.definitionFit: To bother someone is to annoy or trouble them, a verb synonym of upsets.

clue.text: Four start off in play area possibly

indicators.note: off means gone wrong or awry, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Four runners in a race start off in a playground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' scrambles FOURSTART; 'possibly' warns that the definition is only one example of where the surface is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Artificial grass covers sports pitches and play areas, so a play area may be laid with this brand of synthetic turf.

clue.text: We may wish for sweet ones on retirement

definitions.text: We may wish for sweet ones on retirement

parts.words: We may wish for sweet ones on retirement
parts.note: 'retirement' here is going to bed, not leaving work; 'sweet ones' recalls the goodnight wish people say at bedtime

explanation.surface: People leaving their jobs hope for pleasant things in their retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retirement' suggests ending a career, but it means retiring for the night, when we wish each other pleasant visions in sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: The visions experienced in sleep are what a goodnight wish of 'sweet ...' refers to.

clue.text: Speak terribly posh,like company bosses may do

parts.note: to speak is to talk

indicators.note: terribly means badly done, so the letters of posh are jumbled

explanation.surface: Company bosses are mocked for speaking in a dreadfully affected upper-class accent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' rearranges POSH to SHOP. The surface makes 'terribly posh' a description of an accent.
explanation.definitionFit: Executives tend to discuss business matters even in social settings, which is the idiom for chatting about work.

clue.text: Heads lose carbon copies

indicators.note: lose says the carbon letter is dropped from the headlands

parts.note: a head or headland is a cape on a coastline
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: Office heads lose their carbon copies of documents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carbon copies' reads as one phrase; split it, with 'copies' the definition as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to imitate or mimic them, so the verb is a synonym of copies.

clue.text: Kipling's extremes shown in full measure

parts.note: the first and last letters of the writer's name are K and G, the symbol for a unit of mass, which is to be written out as a whole word

explanation.surface: A tribute to Kipling's work shown in its full extent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremes' picks K and G from Kipling; KG is the abbreviation of a metric unit, and 'shown in full' asks for that unit spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the SI base unit of mass, a standard measure of weight.

clue.text: Spirits not good for those entertaining guests

indicators.note: 'not good' tells us the letter for good is removed from the spirits

parts.note: ghosts are spirits of the dead

explanation.surface: Drinks that are not good make a poor choice for people entertaining visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' looks like alcohol, which suits the party scene, but it means phantoms.
explanation.definitionFit: People who receive and entertain guests are the party givers, or hosts in the hospitality sense.

clue.text: Heavy defeat often followed by hanging

definitions.meaning: a thrashing or drubbing in a game
applying glue to wallpaper, which is then hung on the wall

explanation.surface: A heavy defeat in a trial was often followed by execution on the gallows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hanging' suggests the gallows, but it is the hanging of wallpaper, which comes after gluing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A crushing defeat is informally a thrashing; and wallpaper gets glued before it is hung.

clue.text: Bowler, perhaps,for the East Enders

parts.note: Cockneys of London's East End use rhyming slang 'tit for tat' for hat, shortened and pronounced in their accent

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler is perhaps playing for a team from London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowler' suggests cricket but is the hat. Cockney rhyming slang, from London's East End, uses 'tit for tat' for hat, and 'for' is said 'fer'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the slang word for any hat, of which a bowler is one example.

clue.text: Brings in twigs

definitions.meaning: earns or makes money from a sale

explanation.surface: Someone carries small branches indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twigs' looks like a noun for small branches but is the informal British verb meaning grasps.
explanation.definitionFit: A sale converts assets into money, and suddenly understanding something is becoming aware of it.

clue.text: Distinct bulge, oddly, on back of German car

parts.note: Audi is a German make of car

indicators.note: oddly picks out the letters in the odd positions of bulge

explanation.surface: A noticeable dent or bulge appears on the rear of a German car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' takes B, L and E from 'bulge'; 'on back of' places them after AUDI.
explanation.definitionFit: A distinct sound is one clear enough to be heard, a near synonym of the answer.

clue.text: More sound without depth can be colossal

indicators.note: can be suggests the remaining letters may be made into something else, a reordering
without tells us to remove the letter for depth from the phrase

explanation.surface: More sound without depth can be huge, a remark about loud music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes D from MORE SOUND, leaving MORESOUN, and 'can be' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something immense in size, a straightforward synonym pair.

clue.text: Rejected is story of tennis star

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the words is and a story are read backwards

parts.note: a saga is a long story

explanation.surface: A tennis player's life story has been turned down by a publisher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' turns ISSAGA round.
explanation.definitionFit: Andre Agassi was an American tennis champion who won eight Grand Slam singles titles.

clue.text: Blister results from Bannister's first run in stockings

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of the runner's name

parts.note: a ladder is a run in tights or stockings (British usage)

explanation.surface: Roger Bannister, the first four-minute miler, gets a blister running in his socks.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger Bannister ran the first four-minute mile, so 'run' looks athletic, but a ladder is the British word for a run in a stocking.
explanation.definitionFit: A blister is a small fluid-filled sac on the skin, and the word also names any such pouch or vesicle.

clue.text: Avoid car crash but lose time

indicators.note: lose says the letter for time is dropped from the collision

parts.note: a shunt is British slang for a minor collision between cars

explanation.surface: A driver manages to avoid a crash but loses time in the race.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'shunt' is British slang for a bump between vehicles, especially in motor racing.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep away from something or someone deliberately is a synonym of avoid.

clue.text: Girl almost in first place appears deceptive

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the girl is cut

parts.note: a miss is a girl or young woman
leading means ahead of everyone, in first position

explanation.surface: A girl nearly in first place seems to be giving a false impression of the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last S of MISS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that gives a false impression is deceptive, an adjective synonym.

clue.text: Demon, close and threatening

parts.note: an imp is a small demon
a close or conclusion is an ending

explanation.surface: A demon is near at hand and menacing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close' looks like an adjective meaning near, but it is the noun meaning conclusion.
explanation.definitionFit: Something about to happen, especially something bad, is said to loom or be imminent, as a threat does.

clue.text: New York's generous daily medical insurance?

definitions.note: 's stands for is, so the definition reads as New York is

parts.note: big-hearted, so big means generous
the proverb says one of these fruits a day keeps the doctor away

explanation.surface: A question about New York's generous daily medical insurance plan.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'an apple a day keeps the doctor away' makes the fruit daily medical insurance. The 's in New York's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the well-known nickname of New York City.

clue.text: A musical may, without a blonde

indicators.note: without means minus, so the second a is taken out of may

parts.note: a fair lady is a fair-haired woman, a blonde

explanation.surface: A musical may go ahead without a blonde in the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' takes the A out of MAY, leaving MY; 'fair' means blonde-haired.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Lerner and Loewe stage and film musical based on Shaw's Pygmalion.

clue.text: Courtesy shown when the missus welcomes old queen

indicators.note: welcomes means takes in, so the queen goes inside the missus

parts.note: Mrs is the title of a married woman, the missus
Anne was Queen of Great Britain from 1702 to 1714

explanation.surface: A wife shows good politeness when she receives an elderly queen as a guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the missus' is the written title of a married woman, and Anne was the last Stuart monarch of Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Good behaviour and polite conduct, collectively, is what courtesy describes.

clue.text: Our problems usually seem to start with work

indicators.note: to start with picks out the first letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: Our problems usually seem to begin at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to start with' takes O, P, U, S from the starts of four words.
explanation.definitionFit: A composer's numbered work is labelled with this Latin word, a synonym of work.

clue.text: Close relation adopts others like little birds

indicators.note: adopts means takes on, here the relatives coming after the sister

parts.note: sis is short for sister, a close relation
kins are relatives, others of like family

explanation.surface: A family member adopts other relatives just like little birds taking in chicks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adopts' looks like a container signal, but here the relatives simply follow the sister.
explanation.definitionFit: Siskins are small finches with yellow-green plumage.

clue.text: His judgments were crucial to 13, say

definitions.text: His judgments were crucial to 13, say

parts.words: His judgments were crucial to 13, say
parts.note: 13 across is a tennis star, and line calls and rulings made by the match official decide points

explanation.surface: Someone's judgments were vital to an earlier answer.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference to 13 is the tennis player; the official on the high chair rules on points in every match.
explanation.definitionFit: The official who rules on play in tennis or cricket makes judgments that decide players' fortunes.

clue.text: Old Cardinal has modern ideas, it seems

definitions.meaning: a reformed or modern person, a fresh man

explanation.surface: An elderly cardinal seems to have progressive views.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it seems' signals that the second definition is a playful reading of the name split in two.
explanation.definitionFit: John Henry Newman was a Victorian cardinal, and split in two the surname describes a modern, reformed person.

clue.text: Twisted something that's painful

definitions.meaning: coiled or wrapped round, past tense of wind
an injury, a cut or gash

explanation.definitionFit: The past tense of wind means coiled, and an injury to the body is a homograph with a different sound.

clue.text: An Americanism like "steetcar depot"

parts.note: streetcar is American for tram, and a depot at the end of a line is the last stop; split as three words, the answer reads as a word used in America

explanation.surface: A note that 'streetcar depot' is an American expression.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as TERM IN US and it describes an Americanism; 'steetcar' is a misprint of streetcar, the American word for tram.
explanation.definitionFit: A streetcar depot sits at the end of a line, the last station or stop of the route.

clue.text: We shall briefly appear in the spring

definitions.meaning: we shall shortened with an apostrophe
a source of water, as from a fountain

explanation.surface: We will make a short appearance in springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spring' suggests the season, but it is a water source; 'appear in' links the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A spring or source of water from the ground, and the contraction of we shall, share the same letters.

clue.text: Supplied the ultimate in farce and told jokes

indicators.note: the ultimate in means the last letter of farce

parts.note: quipped means made witty remarks

explanation.surface: A comedy writer supplied the final touches of a farce and told jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the ultimate in' takes E from farce.
explanation.definitionFit: To be furnished with what is needed is to be provided, a synonym of supplied.

clue.text: Provider of minimum cover (not for men!)

definitions.text: Provider of minimum cover (not for men!)

parts.words: Provider of minimum cover (not for men!)
parts.note: minimum cover sounds like an insurance policy, but means a very small two-piece swimsuit worn by women

explanation.surface: An insurance company offers the lowest level of cover, but not to men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover' suggests insurance, but it means clothing on the body.
explanation.definitionFit: A scanty two-piece swimsuit worn by women covers the least possible amount of the body.

clue.text: Misshapen empty shell (undyed) is out of the blue

indicators.note: misshapen means badly formed, so the letters are rearranged
empty takes the inside letters away, leaving only the outer ones of shell

explanation.surface: A deformed, hollow shell left in its natural colour seems unexpected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'empty' leaves S and L of shell; 'Misshapen' rearranges SL with UNDYED. 'blue' looks like a colour beside 'undyed', but the phrase means unexpectedly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening without warning comes out of the blue, an idiom for unexpectedly.

clue.text: Condescends, like Old and Young Hamlet for the audience

indicators.note: for the audience means as heard by listeners, so the word is pronounced, not written

parts.note: both the old king and the young prince in Shakespeare's play are Danes, from Denmark

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's ghostly king and his son both stoop to perform for a theatre audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'audience' suggests theatregoers, but it signals a sound-alike: DANES.
explanation.definitionFit: To stoop to do something one thinks beneath one's dignity is to condescend.
